prize_parts.citation: For the chemistry of ionizable lipid nanoparticles that enabled the delivery of nucleic-acid medicines

statement.case_for: Ionizable lipid nanoparticles are a game-changer in the sense I use the word: a molecular design principle (a lipid whose charge depends on pH, so that it binds nucleic acid during formulation and releases it from the endosome) that turned siRNA and mRNA from fragile molecules into practical medicines. The consequences are demonstrated at global scale (Onpattro, the COVID-19 mRNA vaccines), the principle has been reproduced by many independent groups, and the chemistry is straightforward enough to explain in two sentences. The 2023 Medicine prize rewarded the nucleoside modification of the cargo, not the vehicle, so this prize would complete the story rather than repeat it. I would present Cullis as the indispensable core, with Anderson and Langer representing the combinatorial lipid-library and in vivo delivery strand.
statement.case_against: Attribution is the real weakness. Credit is spread over the Vancouver group (Cullis, Hope, Madden, MacLachlan) and the MIT strand (Anderson, Langer), the history includes patent disputes, and any three-person cut excludes people whose work was decisive for the clinical products. A critic can also say that the chemistry is an optimisation of lipid structure and formulation, not a single mechanistic discovery, and that the medical impact may be seen as belonging to Physiology or Medicine. If the committee cannot defend a three-name cut, B045 is the better-supported alternative.

responses.point: Chabes ranks targeted protein degradation first as a programmable use of the ubiquitin-proteasome system with Crews, Deshaies and Handa. He ranks lipid nanoparticles last on his list because credit is distributed across groups and patent disputes, and because the work is an optimisation of lipid structure rather than a mechanistic discovery.
responses.response: I take the attribution point seriously and share it; it is why I name Cullis as the core rather than a settled trio. I disagree that this is only optimisation. The pH-dependent ionizable lipid and the encapsulation and endosomal-escape logic are a design principle, and the proof is that one molecular idea carried both siRNA drugs and mRNA vaccines. Compared with B045, I also note that the delivery chemistry has already produced approved medicines at scale, while no PROTAC has reached that point. I do concede that B045 has the broader opening support and that its Crews and Deshaies core is cleaner than my Anderson and Langer slots.

responses.point: Aili ranks B045 first because degraders move pharmacology from inhibition to event-driven removal, with Handa's cereblon work explaining thalidomide. He also puts B009 fourth and says the 2023 Medicine prize left delivery unrecognised, so there is no precedent conflict.
responses.response: We agree on the 2023 point, which is useful because some colleagues worry about overlap. On B045 I accept the mechanistic appeal of cereblon, but I would ask whether we are recognising two achievements. The PROTAC concept (Crews, Deshaies) and the molecular-glue mechanism (Handa) are distinct strands, and a single three-person citation may blur them. I would be comfortable ranking B045 first only if we can write a precise citation and justify excluding Ciulli and Gray, whose VHL ligands and degrader design made PROTACs work as drugs.

responses.point: Sparr ranks lipid nanoparticles second and credits Cullis, Hope and Madden for the Vancouver work on pH-dependent assembly, encapsulation and fusogenic ionizable lipids. She notes that Anderson, Langer and MacLachlan made major lipid-design contributions, so a configuration excludes important people.
responses.response: This is the most useful disagreement for me. Her trio of Cullis, Hope and Madden reflects the earliest encapsulation and assembly science, whereas my Anderson and Langer slots reflect the later lipidoid libraries and in vivo delivery. I chose mine because the ionizable-lipid design that actually reached patients came through that combinatorial route as well, but I accept that the Vancouver priority is stronger for the underlying principle. I would like us to test whether the committee prefers principle priority (Cullis, Hope, Madden) or delivery to patients (Cullis, Anderson, Langer), and I will move toward whichever has the more defensible record.

responses.point: Somfai ranks Pd-catalysed C-N cross-coupling first, arguing that Buchwald and Hartwig made amination general and practical, that the 2010 prize left it out, and that recognition is overdue with a clean two-person attribution.
responses.response: The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist and I rank B069 seventh only because its scientific consequence seems smaller to me than the new capabilities in biology that other candidates offer. I accept the point about maturity and that the pair is uncontroversial. My reservation is that it extends an area already honoured in 2010, which weighs against the new-and-completely-different standard. I would keep B069 as a safe fallback rather than the leading choice, but I would not oppose it if the committee cannot agree on a delivery or degrader trio.

uncertainties: Fair division of credit among Cullis, Hope, Madden and MacLachlan on one side and Anderson and Langer on the other; I am relying on recollection of the publication and patent history, not verifying it here.
Whether the committee regards ionizable lipid delivery as chemistry or as a medical technology belonging to Physiology or Medicine.
Whether B045 should be preferred once the PROTAC and molecular-glue strands and the exclusion of Ciulli and Gray are considered.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My connections are Arieh Warshel (postdoc collaboration), the Uppsala ribosome community and committee colleagues, and none of the shortlisted candidates falls in those groups.
